pages.name: Fifty units
pages.text: Fifty units sit on a shelf. Each drops off when it fails. Here the clock has run 5 years, and the units that failed have dropped. The strip below reads flat at 0.1 a year. That is the [[failure rate]]: failures each year for each unit still working. Here an old unit is as likely to fail next month as a new one. The shelf empties fastest at first only because more units are there to fail.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated units sit in two rows on a shelf, with a clock's hand on a time axis in years below. Each unit drops onto the axis when it fails and piles up by the year it failed. Under the years, a strip draws the failure rate of the units still working, flat.

pages.name: The next year
pages.task: At 5 years, say 30 units are still working. About how many fail in the next year?
pages.why: The rate counts failures each year for each unit still working. So about 30 × 0.1 = 3 are expected to fail. A few either side is normal. At a steady rate age changes nothing, so the units left are no stronger. A right answer runs the clock on to 6 years.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated units at 5 years in service: some still on the shelf, the rest piled up by the year they failed. The failure rate strip is flat. The clock runs on to 6 years, and a few more units drop off the shelf.
options: About 1, as the weak ones have already gone

pages.name: The share still working
pages.text: The share still working is the [[reliability]], R. Each short spell, the shelf loses the same fraction of what is left. That gives the decay curve you know from a capacitor: R = e^(−λt). At 5 years, R = e^(−0.5), about 0.61. So the rule expects 30.3 of the fifty. [[MTBF]] means mean time between failures. A unit fails 0.1 times for each year it runs. So on average it runs 1 ÷ λ = 10 years to a failure.
pages.alt: The shelf of simulated units at 5 years, with an amber curve over the pile showing what the rule expects, and a dashed line at the MTBF of 10 years.

pages.name: At 10 years
pages.task: The MTBF here is 10 years. At 10 years in service, what share of the units still work?
pages.why: Put t = 10 into the rule: R = e^(−0.1 × 10) = e^(−1), about 0.37. So only about 37% reach the MTBF. Most lifetimes are short, and a few long ones pull the mean up. A right answer runs the clock on to 10 years.
pages.alt: The shelf of simulated units at 5 years, with the rule's curve over the pile and a dashed line at the MTBF. The clock runs on to the MTBF, 10 years, and only about 37% are left on the shelf.
options: Nearly all, as 10 years is their mean life

pages.name: At the MTBF
pages.text: At 10 years, the shelf holds close to the 18.4 the rule expects. That is about 37%, the same 0.37 you meet after one time constant. Most units fail before the mean lifetime. A few long-lived units pull the mean up. A long high tail did the same with insulation resistance. Half have failed by about 7 years. So the MTBF is a rate turned over, not a life to count on.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated units on a shelf, the clock's hand on a time axis in years, each failed unit piled up by the year it failed under the amber curve the rule expects, and a dashed line at the MTBF.

pages.name: Failed by 5 years
pages.task: λ is 0.1 a year. What is the chance one unit has failed by 5 years?
pages.why: At 5 years, R = e^(−0.5), about 0.61. That is the chance a unit still works. So the chance it has failed is 1 − 0.61, about 0.39, or 39%. A right answer runs the clock from 0 to 5 years, and the failed units pile up.
pages.alt: The full shelf of fifty simulated units at 0 years, with a dashed line at the MTBF. The clock runs to 5 years, and the units that failed pile up under the hand.
options: 50%, as 5 years is half the MTBF

pages.name: Pairs in series
pages.text: Here the units work as pairs in series, at 10 years. A pair works only while both units work. A share R of the first units still works. R of those have a working partner. If each unit fails on its own, R × R of pairs still work. That is e^(−2λt). So the rates add to 0.2 a year. The shelf empties twice as fast. The MTBF halves to 5 years. Working case: both work. Failing case: either fails.
pages.alt: The simulated units joined in 25 pairs in series, each pair's two units linked. A pair drops off the shelf when either unit fails, and the failure rate strip reads twice as high.

pages.name: A pump and its starter
pages.task: A pump and its starter are in series. Each has a 0.9 chance of lasting the year. What is the chance the pair lasts the year?
pages.why: Both must last. So take 0.9 of 0.9: 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81. In series the chances multiply, so the pair is less reliable than either part. A right answer runs one year on pairs in series. At 0.1 a year, each unit lasts it with a chance of about 90%.
pages.alt: The simulated units in 25 pairs in series, each pair linked, on a full shelf at 0 years. The clock runs one year, and the pairs that lost either unit drop off.

pages.name: Pairs in parallel
pages.text: Here the units work as pairs in parallel, at 10 years. A pair works while at least one unit works. So work the failing case: both fail with chance (1 − R) × (1 − R). The pair's reliability is 1 − (1 − R)², about 60% at 10 years. The failure rate starts at zero, because one failure leaves a pair working. Two units run, so the first failure comes after 5 years on average. The survivor then runs another 10 on average. So the MTBF is 15 years.
pages.alt: The simulated units in 25 pairs in parallel, each pair held in one harness. A failed unit stays on the shelf, drawn hollow, until its partner fails too. The failure rate strip starts at zero and climbs.

pages.name: Two chargers
pages.task: Two battery chargers run in parallel. Each has a 0.9 chance of lasting the year. What is the chance at least one lasts?
pages.why: Each charger fails with a chance of 0.1. Both fail with a chance of 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01. So at least one lasts with a chance of 1 − 0.01 = 0.99. The 0.18 counts only one working and the other not. It leaves out both working. A right answer runs one year on pairs in parallel. A failed unit stays, held by its partner.
pages.alt: The simulated units in 25 pairs in parallel, each pair in one harness, on a full shelf at 0 years. The clock runs one year. A few units fail and stay on the shelf, held by their partners, so every pair still works.
options: 0.18, one working and the other not

pages.name: The bathtub
pages.text: Real units are rarely steady for life. Units with hidden faults often fail early, so the rate starts high. For most of a useful life it settles low and roughly steady. Then wear-out sets in, and the rate climbs. That shape is the [[bathtub curve]]. This one is a sketch, not measured. The steady model fits only its flat middle.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated units whose failure rate follows a sketched bathtub, drawn under the years: high early, low and steady in the middle years, rising with wear-out. The failures pile up early and late.

pages.name: Two ages
pages.task: Say two units sit in the flat middle of their lives. One has run 8 years, the other 3. Which is more likely to fail next year?
pages.why: In the flat middle the failure rate is steady. So each unit still working has the same chance of failing next year, whatever its age. There a failure comes by chance, not age. A right answer marks the rate at 3 years and at 8 years. The two marks sit at the same height.
pages.alt: The shelf of simulated units at 8 years, with the failure rate flat at 0.1 a year under the years. Two dots on the flat failure rate, at 3 years and at 8 years, sit at the same height.
options: The 8-year unit, as it is older
The 3-year unit, as the older one has proved itself

pages.name: A UPS in series
pages.task: An example UPS has a rectifier, a battery and an inverter in series. Say their failure rates are 20, 10 and 20 per million hours. What is the UPS's MTBF?
pages.why: In series, any part's failure stops the UPS. So the failure rates add: 20 + 10 + 20 = 50 per million hours. The MTBF turns that over: 1,000,000 ÷ 50 = 20,000 hours. A right answer slides the three rates end to end into one total.

pages.name: A shared battery
pages.task: Two UPSs run in parallel from one shared battery bank. Is 1 − (1 − R)² right for the pair?
pages.answer: No, too hopeful, as a battery fault can stop both
pages.why: The parallel rule assumes each unit fails on its own. A shared battery bank breaks that. One battery fault can stop both UPSs at once. So the battery sits in series with the pair, and the pair is less reliable than the rule promises. A right answer shows the battery bank failing and both UPSs stopping.
